claim: mGluRs are class C, synaptic G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that contain large extracellular ligand binding domains (LBDs) and form constitutive dimers.
source: Metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) are class C, synaptic G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that contain large extracellular ligand binding domains (LBDs) and form constitutive dimers.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the structural and functional characteristics of mGluRs, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Single-molecule subunit counting and inter-TMD fluorescence resonance energy transfer measurements in living cells reveal LBD-independent conformational rearrangements between TMD dimers during receptor modulation.
source: Single-molecule subunit counting and inter-TMD fluorescence resonance energy transfer measurements in living cells reveal LBD-independent conformational rearrangements between TMD dimers during receptor modulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-molecule and FRET measurements described in the manuscript.

claim: The experiments lead to a three-state model of TMD activation.
source: Together our experiments lead to a three-state model of TMD activation, which provides a framework for understanding how inter-subunit rearrangements drive class C GPCR activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript, representing an inference from the results.

claim: mGluRs serve as potential drug targets for a wide range of neurological and psychiatric diseases.
source: Based on their central roles in basic synaptic neurobiology along with compelling preclinical and clinical evidence, mGluRs serve as potential drug targets for a wide range of neurological and psychiatric diseases (Nicoletti et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature (Nicoletti et al., 2011).

claim: mGluRs constitutively dimerize in living cells.
source: Furthermore, mGluRs constitutively dimerize in living cells (Doumazane et al., 2011; Levitz et al., 2016), and dimerization is required for glutamate-driven G-protein activation (El Moustaine et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Doumazane et al., 2011; Levitz et al., 2016).

claim: Dimerization is required for glutamate-driven G-protein activation.
source: Furthermore, mGluRs constitutively dimerize in living cells (Doumazane et al., 2011; Levitz et al., 2016), and dimerization is required for glutamate-driven G-protein activation (El Moustaine et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (El Moustaine et al., 2012).

claim: Recent single-molecule imaging studies have provided a dynamic interpretation of existing dimeric LBD crystal structures to provide a model of the intrasubunit and intersubunit rearrangements that mediate the initial stages of mGluR activation.
source: Recent single-molecule imaging studies have provided a dynamic interpretation of existing dimeric LBD crystal structures (Kunishima et al., 2000; Muto et al., 2007; Tsuchiya et al., 2002) to provide a model of the intrasubunit (i.e. LBD closure) and intersubunit (i.e. dimer interface reorientation) rearrangements that mediate the initial stages of mGluR activation (Olofsson et al., 2014) (Levitz et al., 2016; Vafabakhsh et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies (Kunishima et al., 2000; Muto et al., 2007; Tsuchiya et al., 2002; Olofsson et al., 2014; Levitz et al., 2016; Vafabakhsh et al., 2015).

claim: A recent breakthrough cryo-electron microscopy study of full-length mGluR5 showed clear inter-TMD interactions in a glutamate-bound state.
source: A recent breakthrough cryo-electron microscopy study of full-length mGluR5 showed clear inter-TMD interactions in a glutamate-bound state (Koehl et al., 2019), further motivating investigation of inter-subunit coordination.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study (Koehl et al., 2019).

claim: Positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) are thought to primarily modulate agonist-induced activity, but have also been reported to directly elicit receptor activation in full-length receptors.
source: Positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) are thought to primarily modulate agonist-induced activity, but have also been reported to directly elicit receptor activation in full-length receptors.
evidence: This is a statement about the known effects of PAMs, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Isolated mGluR TMDs can initiate G protein signaling in responses to PAMs.
source: It has also been established that isolated mGluR TMDs can initiate G protein signaling in responses to PAMs (El Moustaine et al., 2012; Goudet et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (El Moustaine et al., 2012; Goudet et al., 2004).

claim: Positive allosteric modulators of mGluR2 serve directly as agonists which can drive activation by reorienting TMD dimers independently of allosteric input from the LBDs.
source: Here, we use a battery of electrophysiological and imaging-based assays to show that positive allosteric modulators of mGluR2 serve directly as agonists which can drive activation by reorienting TMD dimers independently of allosteric input from the LBDs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological and imaging-based assays described in the manuscript.

claim: mGluR2 TMD shows a unique, high propensity for dimerization that is not seen in other group I and II mGluR subtypes or in canonical class A GPCRs.
source: Using a single-molecule subunit counting assay, we find that this inter-TMD reorientation is underscored by a unique, high propensity for mGluR2 TMD dimerization that is not seen in other group I and II mGluR subtypes or in canonical class A GPCRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from single-molecule subunit counting assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: mGluR2 PAMs show variable apparent affinity, efficacy, kinetics, and reversibility of mGluR2 modulation.
source: Using a new inter-TMD FRET assay we find that mGluR2 PAMs show variable apparent affinity, efficacy, kinetics, and reversibility of mGluR2 modulation which should inform future applications and drug development.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from inter-TMD FRET assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: NAMs modulate inter-TMD arrangement and can either be neutral antagonists or serve as inverse agonists.
source: We also find that NAMs modulate inter-TMD arrangement and can either be neutral antagonists or serve as inverse agonists.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from inter-TMD FRET and functional assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Application of LY48 to cells expressing mGluR2 and GIRK produced large, reversible inward currents that were up to ~70% in amplitude compared to those induced by saturating glutamate.
source: Application of only LY48 to cells expressing mGluR2 and GIRK produced large, reversible inward currents that were up to ~70% in amplitude compared to those induced by saturating glutamate (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: LY48 responses were blocked by co-application of the mGluR2 negative allosteric modulator (NAM) MNI 137.
source: LY48 responses were blocked by co-application of the mGluR2 negative allosteric modulator (NAM) MNI 137 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: mGluR2-R57A displayed very similar responses to LY48 as wild-type mGluR2.
source: mGluR2-R57A displayed very similar responses to LY48 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) and the LY48 dose–response curves for mGluR2-WT and mGluR2-R57A were identical with both showing maximal PAM-induced activation of ~70% relative to glutamate and an EC50 of ~300 nM (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Co-application of a saturating concentration of LY341495 (LY34), a competitive antagonist that prevents LBD closure, did not prevent mGluR2 activation by LY48.
source: Co-application of a saturating concentration of LY341495 (LY34), a competitive antagonist that prevents LBD closure (Vafabakhsh et al., 2015) did not prevent mGluR2 activation by LY48 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1D and a citation to Vafabakhsh et al., 2015.

claim: Complete removal of the extracellular domain did not prevent LY48-mediated activation.
source: Furthermore, consistent with previous studies (El Moustaine et al., 2012), complete removal of the extracellular domain did not prevent LY48-mediated activation, indicating that an intact LBD is not needed for mGluR2 activation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1E and a citation to El Moustaine et al., 2012.

claim: Saturating concentrations of LY48 were unable to directly induce LBD closure as assayed using an inter-LBD FRET assay.
source: Despite the modulatory effects of the LBD on PAM activation, saturating concentrations of LY48 were unable to directly induce LBD closure as assayed using an inter-LBD FRET assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: SNAP-mGluR2 molecules photobleached primarily in one-step (~40%) or two-step (~60%) events with a small population showing >3 steps (5.5 ± 0.61%).
source: Consistent with previous studies, following immobilization with a biotinylated anti-HA antibody, single SNAP-mGluR2 molecules photobleached primarily in one-step (~40%) or two-step (~60%) events with a small population showing >3 steps (5.5 ± 0.61%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C), consistent with an obligatory dimer with ~80% SNAP labeling efficiency (Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule pulldown data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: SNAP-mGluR2-TMD displayed ~45% of spots bleaching in 2-steps, consistent with a population of ~60% dimers.
source: We next performed the same measurements with SNAP-mGluR2-TMD and observed ~45% of spots bleaching in 2-steps (Figure 2B–D), consistent with a population of ~60% dimers.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule pulldown data shown in Figure 2B–D.

claim: SNAP-mGluR1-TMD, SNAP-mGluR3-TMD and SNAP-mGluR5-TMD all exhibited a lower two-step photobleaching frequency (~30%) compared to SNAP-mGluR2-TMD.
source: Compared to SNAP-mGluR2-TMD, SNAP-mGluR1-TMD, SNAP-mGluR3-TMD and SNAP-mGluR5-TMD all exhibited a lower two-step photobleaching frequency (~30%) (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which suggests that the strength and extent of inter-TMD interaction is mGluR subtype-specific.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule pulldown data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: SNAP-ß2AR showed ~10% two-step photobleaching which is consistent with a pure monomer.
source: We expressed HA- and SNAP-tagged ß2AR ('SNAP-ß2AR') and pulled down surface receptors from HEK 293T cell lysate via the same anti-HA antibody and under identical lysis conditions to the mGluRs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). We observed ~10% two-step photobleaching which is consistent with a pure monomer (Materials and methods) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule pulldown data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Application of PAMs or NAMs to SNAP-mGluR2-TMD did not alter the photobleaching step distributions.
source: We counted SNAP-mGluR2-TMD bleaching steps in the presence of either two different mGluR2 PAMs (LY48 and BINA) or two different mGluR2 NAMs (MNI 137 and Ro 64–2259) and found that the photobleaching step distributions in all cases were similar, with ~40–45% two-step bleaching events (Figure 2E,F; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A) and no change in the proportion of higher order complexes with >3 bleaching steps (<10%).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule pulldown data shown in Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Application of LY48 to SNAP-mGluR2-TMD and CLIP-mGluR2-TMD produced a readily detectable FRET increase, which was reversed with drug washout.
source: Strikingly, application of LY48 produced a readily detectable FRET increase, as determined by a simultaneous increase in acceptor fluorescence and decrease in donor fluorescence, which was reversed with drug washout (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: LY48-induced FRET responses were repeatable, showed no desensitization over 5 min, were blocked by the NAM MNI 137 and dose-dependent over the concentration range used for functional experiments.
source: LY48-induced FRET responses were repeatable (Figure 3C), showed no desensitization over 5 min (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), were blocked by the NAM MNI 137 (Figure 3D) and dose-dependent over the concentration range used for functional experiments (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, Figure 3D, and Figure 3E,F.

claim: Application of the mGluR5 PAM VU0360172 to SNAP-mGluR5-TMD produced a reversible FRET response.
source: To test if LBD-independent inter-TMD rearrangement is a feature of other mGluRs, we asked if donor and acceptor conjugation to SNAP-mGluR5-TMD would allow for the detection a FRET response to a PAM. Application of the mGluR5 PAM VU0360172 produced a reversible FRET response suggesting that, indeed, this conformational assay is generalizable across the mGluR family (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Co-expression of a dominant-negative Gα protein resulted in a substantial left-shift in the inter-TMD FRET dose–response curve.
source: Consistent with this model, when we co-expressed a dominant-negative Gα protein with reduced guanine nucleotide affinity to stabilize the receptor–G protein interaction (Barren and Artemyev, 2007), there was a substantial left-shift in the inter-TMD FRET dose–response curve (Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and a citation to Barren and Artemyev, 2007.

claim: Mutation of asparagine 735 to aspartate (N735D) resulted in drastically reduced activation by LY48 in the GIRK assay.
source: Consistent with our prediction, mutation of asparagine 735 to aspartate (N735D) resulted in drastically reduced activation by LY48 in the GIRK assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: The N735D mutant showed a ~ 20 fold rightward shift in the LY48 inter-TMD FRET dose–response curve compared to the wild-type receptor.
source: Consistent with functional measurements, the N735D mutant showed a ~ 20 fold rightward shift in the LY48 inter-TMD FRET dose–response curve compared to the wild-type receptor (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,E.

claim: All the PAMs tested produced a clear, dose-dependent increase in inter-TMD FRET.
source: Similar to LY48, all the PAMs tested produced a clear, dose-dependent increase in inter-TMD FRET (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: At saturating concentrations, the PAMs produced different maximal FRET changes, as compared to saturating LY48.
source: At saturating concentrations, however, the PAMs produced different maximal FRET changes, as compared to saturating LY48 (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TASP 0433864 produced a maximum FRET increase of ~1.3 times that of LY48, whereas BINA produced an increase only ~0.8 times that of LY48.
source: TASP 0433864 produced a maximum FRET increase of ~1.3 times that of LY48, whereas BINA produced an increase only ~0.8 times that of LY48.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There was no correlation between the apparent PAM affinity and the apparent efficacy, as measured by maximal TMD FRET change.
source: Importantly, there was no correlation between the apparent PAM affinity and the apparent efficacy, as measured by maximal TMD FRET change (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All the tested PAMs modulated the DCG-IV response, but did not alter LBD FRET in the absence of an orthosteric agonist.
source: Similar to LY48, all the tested PAMs modulated the DCG-IV response, but did not alter LBD FRET in the absence of an orthosteric agonist (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The maximal inter-TMD FRET change produced by a given PAM is correlated with its ability to both modulate the agonist response and to directly produce G-protein activation.
source: Strikingly, the maximal inter-TMD FRET change produced by a given PAM is correlated with its ability to both modulate the agonist response (Figure 4I; Figure 4—figure supplement 3B) and to directly produce G-protein activation (Figure 4J; Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET and functional data shown in Figure 4I, Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Xanthurenic acid (XA) did not produce inter-TMD FRET changes or GIRK currents in full-length mGluR2-expressing cells at concentrations up to 50 µM.
source: We applied XA at concentrations up to 50 µM and observed neither inter-TMD FRET changes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) nor GIRK currents in full-length mGluR2-expressing cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET and electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Across all concentrations, both the induction and the reversal of inter-LBD FRET in response to glutamate was faster than the PAM-induced changes.
source: Across all concentrations, both the induction and the reversal of inter-LBD FRET in response to glutamate was faster than the PAM-induced changes (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Saturating LY48-induced GIRK currents were significantly slower than saturating glutamate-induced GIRK currents.
source: Indeed, saturating LY48-induced GIRK currents were significantly slower than saturating glutamate-induced GIRK currents (10 µM LY48 (time 10% to 90%)=14.3 ± 3.5 s versus 1 mM Glutamate (Time 10% to 90%)=1.9 ± 0.5 s; paired T-test, p=0.04).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: BINA showed drastically slower FRET responses that took up to 3 min to reach a steady state and were irreversible on the time scale of measurements for up to 10 min.
source: To our surprise, while saturating concentrations of LY48, CBiPES, and TASP gave rise to clear FRET responses with relatively rapid onset (10–40 s) and reversal (<2 min), BINA showed drastically slower FRET responses that took up to 3 min to reach a steady state and were irreversible on the time scale of our measurements for up to 10 min (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: LY48 showed fully-reversible currents, whereas BINA responses were maintained following up to 10 min of washout in the GIRK activation assay.
source: These distinct kinetics of PAM responses were maintained in our GIRK activation assay where LY48 showed fully-reversible currents, whereas BINA responses were maintained following up to 10 min of washout (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: MNI 137 clearly reversed the BINA-induced FRET increase back to baseline.
source: MNI 137 clearly reversed the BINA-induced FRET increase back to baseline, implying that it indeed can rapidly compete with BINA for a common binding site (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Following washout of MNI 137 a slow FRET increase was observed even though BINA was not reapplied.
source: However, following washout of MNI 137 a slow FRET increase was observed even though BINA was not reapplied.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Of the four PAMs tested, BINA produced the greatest changes in gramicidin channel function (i.e. membrane properties) over a range of concentrations from 1 to 10 µM.
source: Of the four PAMs tested, BINA produced the greatest changes in gramicidin channel function (i.e. membrane properties) over a range of concentrations from 1 to 10 µM (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the gramicidin-based fluorescence assay shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: Application of MNI 137 alone produced minimal FRET changes even at the highest concentrations tested.
source: Application of MNI 137 alone produced minimal FRET changes even at the highest concentrations tested (Figure 6B), suggesting that the resting TMD conformation is not altered, though our sensors may not detect very localized conformational changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 6B (note: this should be Figure 7B based on the manuscript structure).

claim: Ro 64–5229 produced robust, dose-dependent inter-TMD FRET increases with amplitudes comparable to mGluR2 PAMs.
source: In contrast, Ro 64–5229 ('Ro 64') produced robust, dose-dependent inter-TMD FRET increases with amplitudes comparable to mGluR2 PAMs (Figure 7B,C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 7B,C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ro 64 showed similar ON kinetics to LY48, but very slow OFF kinetics that did not fully reverse on the time course of experiments.
source: Interestingly, Ro 64 showed similar ON kinetics to LY48 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), but very slow OFF kinetics that did not fully reverse on the time course of our experiments (Figure 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Neither MNI 137 nor Ro 64 produced changes in gramicidin channel function indicating that they do not alter membrane properties.
source: However, unlike BINA, neither MNI 137 nor Ro 64 produced changes in gramicidin channel function indicating that they do not alter membrane properties (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), despite their hydrophobicity (cLogP ≈ 1.7 for MNI 137 and ≈ 4.9 for Ro 64).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the gramicidin-based fluorescence assay shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Saturating concentrations of either MNI 137 or Ro 64 showed a similar level of partial antagonism of the FRET response to DCG-IV.
source: Saturating concentrations of either MNI 137 or Ro 64 showed a similar level of partial antagonism of the FRET response to DCG-IV (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: MNI 137 showed no effect on basal current in cells expressing GIRK and full-length mGluR2.
source: Whereas MNI 137 showed no effect on basal current (Figure 7D), Ro 64 produced a small but clear outward current (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Ro 64 produced a small but clear outward current in cells expressing GIRK and full-length mGluR2.
source: Whereas MNI 137 showed no effect on basal current (Figure 7D), Ro 64 produced a small but clear outward current (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7E,F.

claim: Ro 64 acts as an inverse agonist while MNI 137 is a neutral antagonist.
source: These data show that Ro 64 acts as an inverse agonist while MNI 137 is a neutral antagonist.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ro 64 did not alter the basal inter-LBD FRET, indicating that it exerts its effects without altering LBD conformation.
source: Despite the effect on basal GIRK activity, Ro 64 did not alter the basal inter-LBD FRET, indicating that it exerts its effects without altering LBD conformation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G), as is also seen with MNI 137 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: MNI 137 was able to partially reverse the inter-TMD FRET increase induced by Ro 64.
source: Consistent with Ro 64 serving as an inverse agonist and MNI 137 serving as a neutral antagonist, MNI 137 was able to partially reverse the inter-TMD FRET increase induced by Ro 64 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1I.
